早期 Xylette 以鋁製音條、夾板、雲杉琴鍵與硬木琴槌製成；Pre-Pian: The early Xylette was made with aluminium tone bars, a plywood frame, spruce keys and hardwood hammers; the Pre-Piano used carbon steel rods instead of strings. Early production models had bodies covered in black Tolex, and the lid was at first fibreglass, changing after 1969 to vacuum-formed plastic. The sounding parts are thin metal tone bars and tines, and after the hammer strikes, a pickup turns the vibration into an electrical signal; the source does not state the materials of other parts.

羅茲電鋼琴以琴鍵驅動小槌敲擊金屬音叉片，音叉片連接到較大的音條，形成類似音叉的振: On the Rhodes the keys drive small hammers that strike thin metal tines; the tines are joined to larger tone bars, so that they vibrate like a tuning fork, and a pickup turns this into an electrical signal. The signal goes through the circuitry to an external keyboard amplifier and speaker, and the suitcase models have a built-in power amplifier. Its timbre is softer than a traditional piano's, and it depends on the relative position of tine and pickup: when the two are close together a bell-like tone appears. It still sounds without an amplifier, but more quietly and with a duller quality. The keyboard is laid out like a traditional piano's, and some models have seventy-three keys rather than eighty-eight. Compared with the Wurlitzer electric piano, the Rhodes sustains longer, while the Wurlitzer has more overtones when played hard, with a biting attack.
羅茲電鋼琴在1970年代廣泛出現於爵士、流行與靈魂樂，也被許多搖滾樂手使用；其頻: The Rhodes was widely heard in jazz, pop and soul in the 1970s and was used by many rock players too; its spectrum leaves room in the vocal range, so it supports a singer well. The source mentions that it was used for teaching, public demonstrations and hotel engagements, and that it became popular again in the 1990s; the suitcase model, with built-in amplifier and tremolo, can be listened to directly.
羅茲電鋼琴由哈洛德·羅茲發明，源於二戰期間他在軍中教導傷兵康復時製造鍵盤樂器的嘗: The Rhodes was invented by Harold Rhodes, growing out of his attempts to build a keyboard instrument while he was teaching wounded soldiers back to health in the army during the Second World War. Development continued after the war; in 1959 Fender began marketing a scaled-down version, and the full-size model appeared in 1965 after Fender sold the business to Columbia Broadcasting System. In the 1970s the company made it in large numbers, and it was widely used in jazz, pop, soul and rock. In the 1980s it was used less, because of competition from polyphonic and digital synthesizers and because of quality-control problems; in 1987 it was sold to Roland, which brought out a digital version, and it revived in the 1990s, with Rhodes taking back the rights in 1997.

The Rhodes is an electrophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 511, from North America. Its keyboard and hammers strike thin metal tines, which are joined to tone bars and vibrate; an electromagnetic pickup turns the vibration into an electrical signal, which passes through the circuitry to an external keyboard amplifier and speaker. Unplugged it still sounds, but more quietly and with a duller timbre. It is played much like a traditional piano, and some models have 73 keys. In the 1970s it was common in jazz, pop and soul, and it was also found among rock players.
